Treasure
TREZH-er
n.
Old French tresor, from Latin thesaurus (treasure, storehouse), from Greek thēsauros. Renders the Hebrew ’ōtsār, “treasure, storehouse,” and segūllāh, “a peculiar treasure,” and the Greek thēsauros, “treasure, treasure-house.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Treasure in Scripture is what the heart accounts most valuable—what is most carefully kept, most fondly returned to, most reluctantly parted with—and Christ Himself sets the diagnostic: for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. The location of one’s actual treasure can be discovered by tracing the location of one’s actual heart, since the two are bound together. The Sermon on the Mount sets the two great treasure-options at maximum contrast: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal. The earthly treasures are characterized by their vulnerability: moth eats, rust corrupts, thieves break through; they cannot be securely held. The heavenly treasures are characterized by their inviolability: nothing in heaven moths, rusts, or steals; what is laid up there cannot be lost. The application is therefore obvious in principle but searching in practice: where the saint deliberately invests his time, money, attention, and energy in the things of heaven (the gospel, the souls of men, the kingdom of Christ, the building up of the church, the relief of the poor, the unseen labors of prayer and faithfulness)—there his treasure is being laid up; and where the saint instead invests these same energies primarily in the things of earth (status, accumulation, comfort, leisure, the building of his own visible empire)—there his treasure remains exposed, and his heart with it. Scripture extends the treasure category in several beautiful ways. Israel is the LORD’s peculiar treasure (segūllāh)—a personal possession of distinct preciousness to the King of all the earth (Ex 19:5); the church inherits the title in 1 Pet 2:9 (a peculiar people). The treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid in Christ (Col 2:3); the gospel itself is the treasure carried in earthen vessels (2 Cor 4:7); the kingdom is the treasure hid in a field for which the man sold all that he had to buy the field (Matt 13:44); the saint is to be like the householder bringing forth out of his treasure things new and old (Matt 13:52). Treasure is therefore a category that organizes much of the Christian life: what the heart treasures, the soul becomes; where the treasure is laid up, the heart follows; what Christ counts as treasure becomes, by the regenerating Spirit, the very things the saint comes to treasure also.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TREASURE as wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve; great quantity of anything collected for future use; in scripture, that which is highly valued and carefully kept; spiritual riches.

TREASURE, n. — 1. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve. 2. Great quantity of anything collected for future use. 3. Anything of much worth; that which is highly valued. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also (Matt 6:21). 4. In scripture, that which is highly valued and carefully kept; spiritual riches; the gospel.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 6:19-21 — "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven... For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Matthew 13:44 — "Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field."

2 Corinthians 4:7 — "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us."

Colossians 2:3 — "In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Treasure is corrupted by the materialist register of the present age that has trained the soul to treasure earthly things primarily and heavenly things vaguely—and by the inverse corruption of certain monastic and dualistic traditions that have denigrated created goods themselves as if they were the very things Scripture warns against treasuring.

expand to see more

The materialist register of late-modern consumer culture is the great contemporary corruption of treasure. The believer is trained from earliest life to identify the good life with accumulation: better house, better car, better retirement portfolio, better experiences, better resume. The very capacity to treasure heavenly things is atrophied by a culture that has reduced the imaginable goods to earthly ones. The diagnostic Christ gives is therefore searching: trace where the saint’s actual time, money, attention, and energy go, and you will find his actual treasure. If they go primarily into earthly accumulation and only marginally into the things of the kingdom, the heart is on earth no matter what the lips confess. The recovery is the deliberate redirection of those energies: time given to prayer and the Word, money given to the relief of the poor and the support of the gospel, attention given to the souls of men, energy given to the unseen labors of faithfulness—and the heart, by the law of treasure, follows.

The opposite corruption is the dualistic or monastic register that has denigrated created goods themselves as if they were the very things Scripture warns against treasuring. Christ does not condemn the having of wealth (Abraham had it, Joseph of Arimathea had it, Lydia had it); He warns against the laying-up of treasure on earth. The created goods—food, drink, beauty, marriage, family, work, play—are gifts of God to be received with thanksgiving, enjoyed in their proper place, and stewarded for the kingdom’s ends. They become treasures-in-the-corrupting-sense only when the heart fastens upon them as its ultimate good. The biblical balance is precise: enjoy God’s gifts as gifts; treasure the Giver and His kingdom as treasure; let the gifts serve the treasure and not displace it; hold the gifts with open hands and the treasure with the whole heart. The man whose hands are full of gifts and whose heart is full of God is the man Scripture commends—and the moth and rust and thief touch nothing he most loves.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ’ōtsār (treasure, storehouse) and segūllāh (peculiar treasure); Greek thēsauros (treasure, treasure-house)—what the heart accounts most valuable; located by the trace of the heart’s actual investment; held secure when laid up in heaven where moth, rust, and thieves cannot reach it.

expand to see more

Hebrew ’ōtsār (H214) — treasure, storehouse.

Hebrew segūllāh (H5459) — peculiar treasure, personal possession (Ex 19:5; Deut 7:6; 14:2; 26:18; Mal 3:17).

Greek thēsauros (G2344) — treasure, treasure-house (Matt 6:19-21; 13:44; 2 Cor 4:7; Col 2:3).

Greek thēsaurizō (G2343) — to lay up treasure (Matt 6:19-20; 1 Cor 16:2; 2 Pet 3:7).

Usage

"For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also—the diagnostic Christ gives for locating the heart’s actual loves."

"Earthly treasure: moth, rust, thief. Heavenly treasure: none of these. The investment-recommendation is obvious in principle and searching in practice."

"Materialism trains the soul to treasure earthly things; dualism denigrates created goods as such; biblical balance enjoys gifts as gifts and treasures the Giver as treasure."
